options.text: It cuts the log to fit the window, and the run goes on.
options.why: Tempting. This board has no cap, so nothing cuts the log.

options.text: The model reads the log in pieces, and the run goes on.
options.why: Tempting. Nothing in this board reads in pieces. The whole log stays in the prompt.

options.text: The next request is too big to send, and the run fails.
options.why: Right. The log comes back whole, and the prompt grows past the window.

outcome: The log came back whole. The next prompt was too big to send, and the run failed.
question: A tool returns a whole log, and the log is bigger than the window. What does the harness do next?

options.text: About 4 tokens.
options.why: Tempting. That reads the rule backwards: four characters make about one token, not four tokens.

options.text: About 10 tokens.
options.why: Right. Forty characters divided by four characters per token is about ten tokens.

options.text: About 40 tokens.
options.why: Tempting. That counts one token per character, which the rule does not say.

question: The course's rule is about four characters per token. About how many tokens is a 40-character line?

options.text: A token is always one word.
options.why: Tempting. Many tokens are words, but not all of them.

options.text: A token can be a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark.
options.why: Right. The tokenizer cuts text where it cuts, and the pieces vary.

options.text: A token is always one character.
options.why: Wrong. A token is usually longer than one character.

question: Which statement about tokens is right?

options.text: Only the earlier messages count against the window.
options.why: Tempting. History is one part. The instructions and the tool results count too.

options.text: All of them share one window, and the reply counts too.
options.why: Right. The window is one desk, and everything on it uses the same space.

options.text: The reply has a separate window of its own.
options.why: Wrong. The reply shares the window with the input.

question: Instructions, earlier messages, tool results and the reply all go into the context window. Which is true?

options.text: A complete answer, with nothing left out.
options.why: Tempting. A reply is complete when the model finishes on its own. This one was stopped by a limit.

options.text: A reply cut short at the output limit.
options.why: Right. The output limit is on the reply itself, so the reply stops early and is not complete.

options.text: An error that says the window is full.
options.why: Tempting. The window is the whole desk. The output limit is only the most one reply may use.

question: A reply stops because it reached its output limit. What does the harness see?

options.text: The reply is cut at the output limit, and the run goes on.
options.why: Tempting. That is the output limit, which caps the reply alone. Here the whole window is what filled up.

options.text: The reply stops early, because the whole window is full.
options.why: Right. The window is the whole desk, shared by the instructions, history, tool results and the reply. When it is full, the reply cannot grow.

options.text: The reply finishes anyway, because the model makes room by itself.
options.why: Wrong. The model does not shrink the window. The harness has to make room before the next call.

question: The whole context window fills before the reply finishes. What happens?

options.text: The bigger call takes longer, and it costs more.
options.why: Right. More tokens means more work. The Sonnet 5.5 price is quoted per million tokens.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the model reads the same text.
options.why: Wrong. The model reads twice as many tokens, so the work doubles.

options.text: The bigger call is faster, because the model has more to go on.
options.why: Tempting. More input is more work for the model, not less.

question: Two calls are the same, but one reads twice as many tokens. Which is most likely true?
